newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Chidambaram sticks by corporate tax.
newsitem.headline: India's Chidambaram sticks by corporate tax.

text.p: Indian Finance Minister P. Chidambaram on Wednesday stood by a controversial minimum tax on corporations, disappointing stock markets which had expected the government to punch loopholes in the proposed measure.
The finance minister defended his tax proposals in parliament, saying they were designed to make industry efficient and pad government resources.

Moving the Finance Bill in the lower house, Chidamabaram said the minimum alternate tax (MAT), a corporate tax he proposed in July when he presented his budget for 1996/97 (April-March), was justified and would not top 12.9 percent.

"I don't propose to raise the tax," Chidambaram said of the levy the government wants to impose on firms that earlier avoided tax payment by making use of a law that enabled tax exemptions on profits if they were ploughed back as investment.
He announced the tax would not apply to companies declared "sick" -- firms whose accumulated losses exceed their net worth.
The tax, which has been stoutly resisted by industry since it was proposed in July, would also not apply to factories located in economically depressed areas, he said.
But he proposed no other changes in the tax, dousing stock markets' hopes.
Share prices finished sharply lower on the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE), which closed before Chidambaram's speech. The 30-share BSE index fell 52.12 points, or 1.52 percent, to 3,382.71.
The 50-stock National Stock Exchange index dropped 10 points to 991.
"The market was expecting some announcement but was disappointed," said one trader.
Traders had been expecting the government to dilute the tax for some sectors like steel and cement.
"The market will seek lower levels if some incentives are not forthcoming," a trader said.

While he kept his tax proposals more or less intact, Chidambaram pressed ahead with his free-trade agenda, cutting import duties and excise taxes on goods ranging from computer parts to steel scrap. The changes will cost the exchequer 940 million rupees, he said.
"There are two major considerations in my proposals," he said. "First to introduce efficiency. Second, the need to raise resources.
"Like the bee sucks honey from the flower, I have tried not to sting or hurt anyone."
